title: Encryption at Rest: KMS & Managed Services 🔑
description: How to protect stored data using AWS Key Management Service and integrated service encryption.

slides.title: Why Encrypt at Rest? 🛌
slides.content:
# Protect Data Where It Lives

Encryption at rest ensures that if someone gains physical access to a disk or a snapshot, the data is unreadable without the key. AWS makes it easy:
- **EBS volumes** can be encrypted with KMS.
- **S3 objects** can use SSE‑S3, SSE‑KMS, or client‑side encryption.
- **RDS and DynamoDB** encrypt data automatically using KMS.
- **EFS** and **FSx** support encryption at rest.

In many cases, encryption can be enabled with a single checkbox. No application changes required.

slides.title: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) 🔐
slides.content:
# The Encryption Backbone

KMS lets you create and manage cryptographic keys (symmetric and asymmetric). Key features:
- **Customer Master Keys (CMKs)**: either AWS managed (free, service‑specific) or customer managed (you control, charges apply).
- **Automatic key rotation** every year for customer managed keys (optional).
- **Fine‑grained permissions**: key policies control who can use the key for encrypt/decrypt.
- **CloudTrail integration**: every key usage is logged.

**Analogy**: KMS is a highly secure vault that stores your keys. When you need to encrypt or decrypt data, you ask the vault to do the operation – the key never leaves the vault.

quizData.question: Which type of KMS key has a key policy that you can edit?

options.text: AWS owned keys (used by default services)

quizData.explanation: Customer managed CMKs give you full control over the key policy, rotation, and lifecycle. AWS managed keys are read‑only for you.

slides.title: Encryption in S3 🔒
slides.content:
# Multiple Options

- **SSE‑S3** – AWS manages the key. Each object is encrypted with a unique key, itself encrypted with a master key. Free.
- **SSE‑KMS** – you control the KMS key, with audit trail and separate permissions. Additional cost.
- **SSE‑C** – you provide the encryption key with each request; AWS doesn't store it.
- **Client‑side encryption** – you encrypt before uploading; AWS never sees plaintext.

Best practice: enable default encryption on every bucket (either SSE‑S3 or SSE‑KMS) and enforce via bucket policy that only encrypted uploads are accepted.

slides.title: EBS Encryption: Transparent & Powerful 💾
slides.content:
# Set It and Forget It

- Encryption uses KMS (AWS managed `aws/ebs` key or a customer managed key).
- When you encrypt a volume, all data at rest, data in flight between instance and volume, snapshots, and volumes created from those snapshots are encrypted.
- You can enable **encryption by default** in each region – all new volumes will be encrypted automatically.
- To encrypt an existing unencrypted volume: snapshot → copy with encryption → create new volume. No direct in‑place conversion.

slides.title: Pro Tip: Use Key Policies for Separation of Duties 👥
slides.content:
## Crypto‑Officer vs User

With KMS, you can separate the person who manages the key (crypto‑officer) from the person who uses it. This prevents a rogue admin from both modifying the key and decrypting data.
